lines: [warmly] Ask. Approve. Try it. Let me show you a different way to get software built... from the client's side.

You've probably been here. You ask for something, and what gets built isn't quite what you meant. It takes weeks, and you only find out at the very end. And now AI can write code in seconds... but who's actually checking it?

That's where a software factory comes in. Think of an assembly line. Every request moves through the same written stages, like a car on a production line. AI agents do the work at each stage... and people step in at the two moments that really matter.

Here's the whole pipeline. The factory reads the request and writes the requirements. You approve. Then it plans, builds, checks, and puts it online. You try it, and approve again. And then it's handed over. Agents do every step... except the two that are yours.

So why should you trust it? Three reasons. Everything is checked twice: a second agent verifies whatever the first one built. Everything is recorded: every check leaves evidence you can actually read. And nothing gets built, or shipped, without a person saying yes.

There are three parts to play. The client asks, approves, and tries the result. The factory writes it down, plans it, builds it, checks it, and puts it online. And your team sets the factory up once... and decides what ships.
Enough talk. Let's watch one real request, from start to finish. A client wants a CRM dashboard... and everything you're about to see actually happened.
Let's start where the client starts. Asking.
Every client gets a private project of their own.
This is their app today. Just an empty page, waiting for its first request. And it sits behind a login only they have.
And here's their project in GitLab. This one project is all they see on the server.
Now, they ask for something.
They open a new issue. The template asks two simple questions: what should change, and how will you know it works? Here, they want a CRM dashboard, with customers in a table and totals at the top.
They hit Create. The template adds the factory label... and that's what hands the request over.
Next, the factory writes it down.
First, it picks the request up.
Within a minute, it comments on the issue. Picked up, requirements written, and now it's waiting for a person. It reports every step like this, out in the open.
Then it stops, and says exactly what it needs: read the requirements, and reply approve.
So, what did it understand?
An agent read the request and the code, and wrote it all down as requirements.
Each story comes with acceptance checks. Every later step is held to these, so the client is agreeing to something specific.
The client also gets a status page. Plain words, five steps, and whose turn it is. Right now, it's theirs. And one button takes them straight to the conversation.
Approving takes one word.
They just reply: approve. And that comment kicks off the next step, right away.
Now the real work. Building, and checking.
It plans, it builds, and it checks.
First, a plan. The work is split into sections, and every section ends with a check that can actually be run.
One agent, the maker, builds a section. A different agent, the checker, verifies it. The checker never saw the maker work. And if something fails, the work goes back with written notes.
The checker writes down its evidence: every check it ran, what it expected, and what it found. And that evidence travels with the change.
Then the whole change is checked again, the tests run, and it's put online for the client to try.
And now, the fun part. Trying it.
They get to use the real thing.
The factory stops again, and posts a link: Try it.
The status page says the same. Built, checked, and it's their turn.
And here it is. The CRM dashboard they asked for, running right there in the browser. Built from one short paragraph.
Totals at the top, every customer at a glance. Just what the issue asked for... and just what the requirements checked.
Then, they approve again.
Happy with it? They reply approve. And that's the second, and last, thing they type.
Finally, the hand-over.
A merge request opens.
The factory opens a merge request, with the code, the tests, the specs, and the checker's evidence, all linked to the issue. Then someone on your team reviews it, and merges it.
The status page shows it's done. Every step ticked, with links to the conversation, the change, and the finished work.
And the whole story stays on the issue. Every step, every check, every approval, all in one place.

So what does all this mean? For clients: they ask in plain words, they can see progress any time, and they try the result before it's final. For your team: one consistent process, written proof of every check... and you still decide what ships.

And this run, in numbers. Seventeen minutes from request to merge request, approvals included. Two words typed by the client. Four sections, and every one passed its checker the first time. And nothing you saw was mocked.
And one factory can serve lots of clients. Each one gets their own project, their own pipeline, and their own previews and status page, behind their own login.
Adding a new client takes one command. It creates the project, the pipeline, the login, and the links to share.
[warmly] Want to try it yourself? Ask for a project of your own, file a small request... and watch it get built.
